question: Company has ROA 8%, cost of debt 10%. Increasing leverage will:
before: When ROA (8%) < cost of debt (10%), every rupee borrowed earns less than it costs. 2% gap comes from shareholders pockets. ROE only increases from leverage when ROA exceeds cost of debt.
after:
Formula: ROE = (ROA + (ROA - Rd) × D/E) where ROE = return on equity, ROA = return on assets (8%), Rd = cost of debt (10%), D = debt, E = equity. The DuPont leverage component (ROA - Rd) × D/E amplifies returns only when positive.

Step-by-step: With ROA = 8% and Rd = 10%, the spread (ROA - Rd) = 8% - 10% = -2%, which is negative. As the company increases leverage (raises D/E ratio), this negative spread gets multiplied by a larger D/E value, making the entire leverage term more negative. This subtracts increasingly from the base ROA, reducing overall ROE.

Why this is correct: When a company borrows at 10% but deploys capital that only earns 8%, each additional rupee of debt financing costs more than it generates. Leverage amplifies this loss rather than gains. Increasing leverage under this condition destroys shareholder value, pushing ROE below even the base ROA.

Why the others are wrong: A assumes leverage always amplifies returns, ignoring the critical condition that ROA must exceed Rd for positive amplification. C overlooks the mechanical impact of the leverage multiplier on returns. D suggests a nonlinear relationship, but the formula shows a linear negative effect throughout — ROE worsens monotonically as D/E rises.

Intuition: In equity research, you must always check the ROA-versus-cost-of-debt spread before assessing leverage decisions. A company with weak returns should deleverage, not add debt, because financial leverage is a double-edged sword. When the sword is dull (ROA < Rd), it cuts the owner's hand.
